subcards.title: Finance Commission (Art 280) and State Finance Commission
subcards.summary: Who divides tax money between the Centre, states and local bodies, and how.
at_a_glance: Art 280 and Art 281 (Union Finance Commission); Art 243I and Art 243Y (State Finance Commission)
The President sets up the Union Finance Commission; the Governor sets up the State Finance Commission. Both every 5 years
A chairman and 4 members; qualifications fixed by a law of 1951
Gives advice only (not binding); quasi-judicial (works like a court); not a permanent body
First Finance Commission set up in 1951; chairman K.C. Neogy
Chairman Arvind Panagariya; period 2026–31; gives 41% of the divisible pool to states

blocks.title: Constitutional basis
head: Item
Fact
rows: Art 280 creates the Finance Commission. Art 281 deals with its recommendations. Both are in Part XII (Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits).
The President, every fifth year, or earlier if the President thinks it necessary.
No. It is a temporary body. A new Commission is set up for each period. (The Rajamannar Committee wanted it made permanent.)
A constitutional body, described as quasi-judicial (works like a court: hears all sides and decides fairly). Its advice is NOT binding.
Set up in 1951. First chairman: K.C. Neogy.
The 'balancing wheel of fiscal federalism' (it keeps money fairly balanced between the Centre and the states).

blocks.title: Composition
head: Item
Fact
rows: A chairman and four other members = 5 in all. All appointed by the President.
Parliament, by law, decides the qualifications and the manner of selection (Art 280(2)). Not the President.

1) a High Court judge or a person qualified to be one; 2) a person with special knowledge of the finance and accounts of government; 3) a person with wide experience in financial matters and administration; 4) a person with special knowledge of economics.
The President fixes the term in the appointment order. The Constitution does not fix 5 years. Members are eligible for reappointment.

blocks.title: Advisory nature
items: Its recommendations are only advice. The Union government is not legally bound to accept them, and states get no legal right to the money recommended.
Reason: the Constitution only asks the President to lay the report before Parliament with a memorandum on action taken. It never says the advice is binding.
Dr P.V. Rajamannar (chairman, 4th Finance Commission): since it is a quasi-judicial constitutional body, its advice should not be rejected 'unless there are very compelling reasons'.

Till 2014 its role was weakened by the Planning Commission, a body that was neither constitutional nor statutory (not made by any law). In 2015 the Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog (also not a constitutional body).

blocks.title: Functions under Art 280(3) — recommendations to the President
head: Clause
What it recommends
rows: How the net proceeds of shareable Union taxes are divided between the Centre and the states together (this is vertical devolution), and how the states' part is then divided among individual states (this is horizontal devolution).
Principles for grants-in-aid to states out of the Consolidated Fund of India (Art 275 grants).

Measures to increase a state's Consolidated Fund so that the state can give more money to its panchayats. These measures must be based on the recommendations of that state's own State Finance Commission.
The same measures for municipalities, again based on the State Finance Commission's recommendations.
Any other matter the President refers to it 'in the interests of sound finance'.
blocks.note: Clauses (bb) and (c) were not in the original 1950 Constitution; they were added in 1992. Till 1960 the Commission also advised on grants to Assam, Bihar, Odisha and West Bengal, given to them in place of a share of the jute export duty.

blocks.title: Two kinds of devolution
head: Aspect
Vertical devolution
Horizontal devolution
rows: The share of the divisible pool (the central taxes that are shared) that goes to all states together
How that combined share of the states is split among the individual states
A formula using income distance, population, area and other criteria

blocks.title: Divisible pool (taxes shared with states, Art 270)
items: Includes all Union List taxes such as income tax, corporation tax and Central GST.
It excludes cesses and surcharges levied by the Union (surcharges under Art 271 go only to the Centre). It also excludes taxes under Art 268, Art 269 and Art 269A.
Since the 80th Amendment (2000), all central taxes (not only income tax and Union excise) are shareable.
Under Art 279, the 'net proceeds' of a tax (the amount left after collection costs) are worked out and certified by the CAG (Comptroller and Auditor General). That certificate is final.

blocks.title: What the Finance Commission does NOT do
items: It does not allow withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund of India.
It does not decide money from the Public Account of India.
It does not suggest ways to increase the Consolidated Fund of India (only a state's Consolidated Fund, for local bodies).
It does not keep the income and expenditure accounts of governments. It does not prescribe the form in which accounts are kept. It does not check whether taxes are levied as the budget provides.
It does not approve the plan spending (plan outlays) of states; that was the Planning Commission's job.
It has nothing to do with foreign capital, public sector undertakings or 'transparency in administration'.

steps.step: 1. President constitutes the Finance Commission (Art 280)
2. Commission submits its report to the President
3. Government prepares an explanatory memorandum on the action taken
4. President lays the report and the memorandum before each House of Parliament (Art 281)

blocks.title: Horizontal devolution weights
head: Criterion
14th (2015–20)
15th (2021–26)
16th (2026–31)
rows: Income distance (how far a state's per-person income is below the richest state's)
Forest cover (14th); forest and ecology (15th and 16th)
Demographic performance (reward for controlling population growth)
Contribution to GDP (new criterion in the 16th)

blocks.title: Why these changes matter
items: The 15th Finance Commission used only the 2011 population. Southern states, which had controlled their population, felt they were losing share. So the 15th added 'demographic performance' (12.5% weight) to reward them.

Besides population, area and income distance, the 15th used three criteria: demographic performance, forest and ecology, and tax and fiscal effort. 'Governance reforms' and 'stable government' were not criteria.
The 15th reduced the states' share from 42% to 41% mainly because Jammu and Kashmir stopped being a state and became Union Territories (2019).
The 16th dropped 'tax and fiscal effort' and added 'contribution to GDP', to reward states that produce more of the country's income.

blocks.title: Other 14th and 15th Finance Commission facts
items: 14th: raised the states' share from 32% to 42%. It did NOT recommend sector-specific grants (grants tied to a particular sector such as health or roads).
14th: grants to gram panchayats were split into a basic grant and a performance grant in the ratio 90 : 10.

15th: ₹4,800 crore (2022–23 to 2025–26) to reward states that improve education outcomes. It also kept ₹45,000 crore as a performance incentive for states that carry out agricultural reforms. And it brought back 'tax and fiscal effort' as a criterion.
The 15th never recommended 45%. Its share for states was 41%.

blocks.title: State Finance Commission
head: Item
Fact
rows: Art 243I (panchayats, Part IX). Art 243Y (municipalities, Part IXA) says the same commission formed under Art 243I also reviews municipal finances.
Art 243I was added by the 73rd Amendment, 1992. Art 243Y was added by the 74th Amendment, 1992
The Governor (that is, the state government), every five years. Not the President.
Not fixed by the Constitution. The State Legislature decides by law its composition, members' qualifications and selection.
The Governor, along with a memorandum of action taken. Not the Chief Minister
Its first State Finance Commission was constituted in 1994 (22 June 1994)

blocks.title: It recommends to the Governor
items: Principles for sharing the net proceeds of state taxes, duties, tolls and fees between the state and the local bodies, and among local bodies of all levels.
Which taxes, duties, tolls and fees may be assigned to local bodies.
Grants-in-aid to local bodies from the state's Consolidated Fund.
Measures to improve the finances of local bodies. Also any other matter the Governor refers to it.
It does NOT audit local body accounts (the State Legislature makes the law on audit). It does NOT divide Union taxes among states (that is the Union Finance Commission's job).

blocks.title: Link with the Central Finance Commission
items: The Central Finance Commission suggests measures to increase a state's Consolidated Fund for its local bodies only on the basis of that state's State Finance Commission recommendations (Art 280(3)(bb) and (c)).
Art 243H separately lets the State Legislature authorise panchayats to levy taxes and tolls.
The 73rd Amendment requires a State Finance Commission (Art 243I) and a State Election Commission (Art 243K). District Planning Committees (Art 243ZD) come from the 74th Amendment, not the 73rd.

blocks.title: Committees on the Finance Commission
items: Rajamannar Committee (set up by Tamil Nadu, 1969): it said the Finance Commission should be made a permanent body and the Planning Commission should be disbanded.

Punchhi Commission: wanted better coordination between the Finance Commission and the Planning Commission; an expert committee to study the plan and non-plan distinction; and removal of the constitutional ceiling on profession tax.
Art 307 (an authority for inter-state trade and commerce) has never been used. Art 280 (Finance Commission), by contrast, is used every five years.

blocks.text: Why the Finance Commission is needed: the Constitution gives more financial power to the Union. So the Finance Commission is needed to keep a financial balance between the Union and the states.
See also: CAG (Art 148, and its Art 279 certificate of net proceeds)
See also: Public Service Commissions (UPSC report under Art 323)

items: The Finance Commission is under Art 280, not Art 263 or Art 290. Its recommendations are dealt with in Art 281. Both are in Part XII.
It has 5 members (a chairman and 4 others). Parliament fixes their qualifications by law, not the President. The chairman needs 'experience in public affairs'.
It is advisory and quasi-judicial: its advice is not binding. The President lays its report, with a memorandum on action taken, before each House of Parliament.
It is not permanent: it is constituted every fifth year or earlier. The members' term is fixed by the President's order, and they can be reappointed.
Its help to local bodies is based on the State Finance Commission's recommendations. This role was added in 1992, not in 1950.
State Finance Commission: set up by the Governor every 5 years under Art 243I. Its composition is decided by the State Legislature. The Governor lays its report.
States' shares: 12th 30.5%, 13th 32%, 14th 42%, 15th 41%, 16th 41%. The 16th did not raise it to 45%.

16th Finance Commission: chairman Panagariya; constituted December 2023; report on 17 November 2025; period 2026–31 (not 2025–30); new criterion 'contribution to GDP' (10%); tax effort dropped; revenue deficit grants stopped.
It is the President (not the Speaker) who lays such reports before Parliament. The report of the PAC (Public Accounts Committee) is Parliament's own report, so the President does not lay it.

subcards.title: Union and State Public Service Commissions (Art 315–323) and Joint PSC
subcards.summary: Who appoints, removes and protects PSC members, and what PSCs do.
at_a_glance: Art 315–323, Part XIV (same Articles for UPSC and State PSCs)
UPSC and State PSC: constitutional bodies. Joint State PSC: statutory body (made by an Act of Parliament)
UPSC: President. State PSC: Governor. Joint State PSC: President
Only the President, for every PSC (Art 317) — never the Governor, even for a State PSC
6 years or age 65 (UPSC); 6 years or age 62 (State PSC and Joint PSC), whichever comes first
Central recruiting agency. Its advice is only advisory — the government need not follow it
Government of India Act 1919 first provided for it; the first PSC was set up in 1926 on the Lee Commission's advice
UPSC Chairman: Dr Ajay Kumar (since May 2025). APPSC Chairperson: A.R. Anuradha (since Oct 2024)

items: UPSC (Union Public Service Commission) is the central recruiting agency of India — it selects people for Union government jobs through exams and interviews.
It is an independent constitutional body — 'constitutional' means the Constitution itself created it.
Each state has its own State Public Service Commission (SPSC, also called State PSC). The same Articles (Art 315 to Art 323, in Part XIV) cover both UPSC and State PSCs.
The Constitution sees the Public Service Commission (PSC) as the 'watch-dog of the merit system' — it guards the rule that government jobs go to the most able candidates.

blocks.title: Acting chairman (added by 15th Amendment, 1963)
items: One of the members is made acting chairman in only two cases: (1) the chairman's post falls vacant, or (2) the chairman cannot work because of absence or another reason (for example, abroad for treatment).
A new member joining is NOT a reason to appoint an acting chairman.
The acting chairman works until a new chairman takes charge or the chairman returns.

Yes — President must refer it to the Supreme Court

steps.step: President refers the charge to the Supreme Court
steps.detail: Even for a State PSC member, the President (not the Governor) makes the reference

steps.step: During the inquiry the member can be suspended
steps.detail: UPSC member: by the President. State PSC member: by the Governor

steps.step: Supreme Court inquires and advises
steps.detail: This advice is binding — the President must follow it

steps.step: If the Supreme Court upholds the charge, the President removes the member

blocks.title: What counts as 'misbehaviour' (defined in the Constitution)
items: Being concerned or interested in any contract or agreement made by the Government of India or a state government.

Taking part in the profit or benefit of such a contract. EXCEPTION: being an ordinary shareholder of a registered (incorporated) company that has such a contract, and sharing profit equally with other shareholders, is NOT misbehaviour.

blocks.title: Cases
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Appointing a university professor who was blind as a State PSC member cannot be set aside on the ground of infirmity of body or mind
Physical disability alone is not a bar to membership

The President referred the case of an Arunachal Pradesh PSC member (after the 2022 exam paper leak) to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court said misbehaviour under Art 317 is personal, not collective: it needs proof of what that member himself did. So it did not advise removal (the reference was rejected).
A member cannot be removed just because the Commission as a whole failed

blocks.title: Safeguards (same pattern for UPSC and State PSC)
items: Security of tenure: removed only in the manner and on the grounds in the Constitution.
Conditions of service (salary, leave, pension and so on) cannot be changed to harm the member after appointment.

All expenses — salaries, allowances and pensions of members and staff — are charged on the Consolidated Fund (of India for UPSC; of the State for a State PSC). 'Charged' means the legislature cannot vote to cut them (Art 322).
After leaving office, members are barred from most further government jobs (Art 319) — see the table below.
No second term: after one full term, a chairman or member cannot be reappointed to the same office.

blocks.note: A UPSC member who becomes UPSC chairman gets a fresh term in the new office: 6 years or till age 65, whichever is earlier.

head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters

Art 319 bar does not stop appointment as Governor (Laxmikanth links this ruling to former UPSC chairman A.R. Kidwai becoming Governor of Bihar)

blocks.title: Functions of UPSC (Art 320)
items: Conducts examinations for the All-India Services (such as IAS and IPS), the Central Services (Group A and Group B) and the public services of Union Territories.
If two or more states request it, UPSC helps them frame and run joint recruitment schemes for services that need candidates with special qualifications.
UPSC can serve any need of a state only when the Governor requests it AND the President approves (Art 315).

When consulted, it advises on: (1) methods of recruitment; (2) principles for appointments, promotions and transfers, and whether candidates are suitable; (3) disciplinary matters of civil servants, including their memorials and petitions (written appeals); (4) claims of a civil servant for legal costs when sued for acts done on official duty; (5) pension claims for injuries suffered on duty; (6) any other matter the President refers to it.
Sends an annual report on its work to the President (Art 323).

blocks.title: Functions of State PSC
items: Main job: conducts examinations for appointments to the state services.
It is consulted on the same list of matters as UPSC, but for state employees. For a State PSC, 'any other matter' is referred by the Governor (not the President).

Under Art 234, when the Governor frames rules for appointing judges of the state judicial service (other than district judges), the Governor must consult both the State PSC and the High Court. Example: rules for Civil Judges (Junior Division) in Andhra Pradesh need consultation with both APPSC and the AP High Court.

blocks.title: Who can extend the functions? (Art 321)
head: Aspect
UPSC
State PSC
rows: Can bring the staff of a local body, a corporate body (for example a public sector corporation) or a public institution under the PSC
Yes, by Act of the state legislature (for example a municipal corporation)

head: Matter
Note
rows: Reservation of posts for backward classes

Art 320(4) says PSCs need not be consulted on reservations made under Art 16(4). The government itself decides how to reserve, the roster points (which vacancy goes to which category) and the number of reserved vacancies
Claims of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in appointments
Art 335 — claims of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes must be considered, while keeping administration efficient
Not consulted only when BOTH are true: the person will hold the post for not more than one year, AND the need is so urgent that asking UPSC would cause undue delay
Most posts in Group C and Group D Central Services
This exclusion is listed for UPSC only
Chairmen and members of boards, commissions and tribunals
This exclusion is listed for UPSC only
Heads of Indian missions abroad (Ambassadors, High Commissioners and similar posts)
This exclusion is listed for UPSC only

blocks.title: Exemption regulations
items: For All-India Services and Central Services, the President can make regulations listing the matters on which UPSC need not be consulted. Example: the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations, 1958.
These regulations must be placed before each House of Parliament for at least 14 days. Parliament CAN amend or cancel (repeal) them.
For state services, the Governor makes such regulations. They are placed before the state legislature for at least 14 days, and the legislature can amend or cancel them.

blocks.title: What UPSC handles vs does not
head: Aspect
Concern of UPSC
Not its concern (handled by DoPT at the Centre; in a state, by the Department of Personnel or the General Administration Department)
rows: Recruitment; advice on promotion and disciplinary matters when consulted
Classification of services, pay and service conditions, cadre management (posting and strength of each service) and training

blocks.title: Advisory nature — Supreme Court rulings
items: PSC advice is only advisory, not binding. The government may accept or reject it.

If the government does not consult the PSC, the affected civil servant cannot get the decision cancelled in court. The Supreme Court calls consultation under Art 320 'directory, not mandatory' — it should be followed, but skipping it does not make the decision invalid.
Being selected by UPSC or a State PSC does not give the candidate a legal right to the post. But the government must act fairly — not arbitrarily and not with bad intention (mala fides).

At the Centre, if the government wants to depart from UPSC's advice on an appointment, the case must go to the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) for decision; a ministry cannot reject it on its own (DoPT rules).

In the recruitment process, UPSC's final step is taken as 'certification' (UPSC certifies and recommends the candidate; the government makes the appointment). This is the answer in a Laxmikanth previous-year question.

head: Office

rows: No fixed term; pleasure of the President

blocks.text: See the Attorney General and Advocate General card

items: State PSC: the Governor appoints, but only the President removes. The Governor can only suspend a member while the Supreme Court inquiry is going on.
Supreme Court's advice on misbehaviour is BINDING on the President. Insolvency, outside paid work and infirmity need no Supreme Court reference.
Age limits: UPSC 65; State PSC and Joint PSC 62 (it was 60 before the 41st Amendment, 1976). The term is 6 years for all.
Joint PSC is statutory — Parliament makes it by law when the state legislatures request. The President appoints its members and receives their resignations.
UPSC Chairman gets no further government job; a UPSC member can become UPSC or State PSC chairman only.
For UPSC to serve a state, both are needed: the Governor's request and the President's approval.
Functions are extended by Parliament (UPSC) or the state legislature (SPSC) — not by the President.
Four limits on PSCs: (1) not consulted on reservations; (2) its advice is not binding; (3) not consulting it does not cancel a decision; (4) being selected gives no legal right to the post.

subcards.title: Comptroller and Auditor General of India (Art 148–151)
subcards.summary: Who audits government money, how the CAG is kept independent, and its limits.
at_a_glance: Articles 148 to 151, in Part V (the Union part) of the Constitution
The President, by a warrant (formal order) under his hand and seal
6 years or age 65, whichever comes first
Same way as a Supreme Court judge: both Houses of Parliament must pass a resolution by special majority
Equal to a Supreme Court judge; charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (paid without a vote of Parliament)
CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971
Indian Audit and Accounts Department (IAAD). The CAG is a one-person (single-member) office
K. Sanjay Murthy, since 21 Nov 2024 (as of Nov 2026)

blocks.title: Articles on the CAG (Part V of the Constitution, the Union part)
head: Article
Subject
rows: Comptroller and Auditor General of India (the office itself)
Duties and powers of the CAG
Form in which accounts of the Union and the States are kept

blocks.title: Why the office matters
items: The CAG is an independent constitutional office set up by Article 148. It is a one-person office (single-member), not a commission.
The CAG heads the Indian Audit and Accounts Department (IAAD). The IAAD itself was created in British times, in 1753.
Called the 'guardian of the public purse': the CAG checks how both the Centre and the States spend public money.
Dr B.R. Ambedkar said the CAG 'shall be the most important officer under the Constitution of India'.
The CAG is one of the bulwarks (strong defenders) of democracy, along with the Supreme Court, the Election Commission and the UPSC.
The Constitution lays down NO qualification for appointment as CAG.

Other bodies and their Articles (often matched with the CAG's Article 148): Election Commission – Article 324; Finance Commission – Article 280; Union Public Service Commission – Article 315; Attorney General – Article 76; Advocate General of a State – Article 165; Governor of a State – Article 153.

steps.step: Appointment
steps.detail: By the President, by a warrant under his hand and seal (Article 148).

steps.step: Oath
steps.detail: Taken before the President. The form of the oath is in the Third Schedule. He swears to uphold the Constitution and the laws and to do his duty without fear or favour.

steps.step: Term
steps.detail: 6 years or until age 65, whichever comes earlier.

steps.step: Resignation
steps.detail: Any time, by a letter addressed to the President. No approval of Parliament is needed.

steps.step: Removal
steps.detail: By the President, in the same manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court judge: proved misbehaviour or incapacity, after a resolution passed by each House of Parliament with special majority (majority of total membership AND two-thirds of members present and voting). The President cannot remove him simply on ministers' advice.

blocks.title: Compare tenures (often matched in exams)
head: Office
Tenure
rows: Member of a State Public Service Commission
Chairperson of the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)
No fixed term; holds office during the pleasure of the President
President, Vice-President, Member of Lok Sabha
5 years each, so the CAG's 6-year term is the longest among these

blocks.text: see Attorney General and Advocate General (Art 76, 165)
see Public Service Commissions for PSC member tenure

blocks.title: How the Constitution keeps the CAG independent
head: Safeguard
What it means
rows: Removable only by the constitutional procedure. So, though appointed by the President, he does NOT hold office at the President's pleasure.

After leaving office he cannot hold any office under the Government of India or of any State (for example, he cannot become a Governor). This removes any reason to please the government while in office.
Salary and service conditions are fixed by Parliament by law (not by the President). By the 1971 Act, his salary equals that of a Supreme Court judge.
After appointment, his salary and rights about leave, pension and age of retirement cannot be changed to his disadvantage. So Parliament cannot cut his term midway.
Service conditions of IAAD staff and the CAG's administrative powers are prescribed by the President after consulting the CAG.

His salary, allowances and pension, and the administrative expenses of his office (including salaries and pensions of IAAD staff), are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. Parliament may discuss them but does NOT vote on them, so no cut motion (a motion to reduce the amount) is possible.
No minister represents the CAG in Parliament, and no minister can be made answerable for his actions. The Finance Minister does NOT represent him.

blocks.title: Related facts
items: The CAG's emoluments (salary, leave and pension terms) are listed in Part E of the Second Schedule of the Constitution.
The CAG is not a member of Parliament and does not take part or vote in Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha sittings.

Removal like a Supreme Court judge also applies to the Chief Election Commissioner (Article 324(5)). The other Election Commissioners can be removed only on the CEC's recommendation, so they do NOT have the same protection.

blocks.title: Other items charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (secondary)
items: Emoluments of the President; salaries of the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha and of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha.
Salaries, allowances and pensions of Supreme Court judges; pensions of High Court judges.
Salary, allowances and pension of the CAG, and of the UPSC chairman and members.
Administrative expenses of the Supreme Court, the CAG's office and the UPSC.
Debt charges (interest and repayment of loans); any sum to satisfy a court judgement or award; anything else Parliament declares charged.
The Prime Minister's salary is NOT charged; it is voted.

blocks.text: Article 149 lets Parliament fix the CAG's duties and powers. Parliament did this through the CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971.

blocks.title: What the CAG audits
head: Area
Detail
rows: All spending from the Consolidated Fund of India, of each State, and of each Union Territory that has a Legislative Assembly
All transactions of the Contingency Fund and Public Account of India and of each State
Trading, manufacturing and profit-and-loss accounts, balance sheets, etc. kept by Central and State departments
Receipts and spending of bodies mostly (substantially) funded from Central or State revenues. Also bodies that get government grants or loans for a specific purpose
All receipts of the Centre and States, to check that tax assessment and collection rules work
Stores and stock kept in Central and State government offices
Under the Companies Act (see Section 5 for how)
Those whose own statute (Central or State law) provides for CAG audit
Any other body when the President or a Governor asks, for example local bodies

blocks.title: Other duties
head: Duty
Detail
rows: Accounts of the Union and States are kept in the form the President prescribes on the CAG's advice. Not the Finance Commission, not the Finance Minister.

The CAG ascertains and certifies the 'net proceeds' of any tax or duty (tax collected minus cost of collection). His certificate is final. (The Finance Commission then recommends how these net proceeds are shared between the Centre and the States; it does not prescribe the form of accounts.)
Submitted to the President, who has them laid before both Houses of Parliament
Submitted to the Governor, who has them laid before the State Legislature (not given to the Chief Minister or Speaker)
Acts as the 'guide, friend and philosopher' of Parliament's Public Accounts Committee
Still compiles and maintains the accounts of State governments

Relieved of compiling Central Government accounts in 1976, when accounts were separated from audit ('departmentalisation of accounts'). This was an administrative change, not a constitutional amendment.

blocks.title: Powers during audit
items: Inspect any office or department under his audit.
Examine all transactions and question the officer in charge.
Call for any records, papers and documents.
Decide the extent and manner of audit.
He has NO power to prosecute or punish anyone. His reports are only information; others (Parliament, investigating agencies) act on them.

blocks.title: Local body audit (secondary)
items: Under Article 243Z, the State Legislature, by law, provides for the maintenance and audit of municipal accounts (Article 243J does the same for panchayats). The CAG audits them only if the State law or a Governor's request brings him in.

sections.heading: 4. Types of audit, reports and the PAC

blocks.title: Types of audit
head: Type
What it checks
Obligatory?
rows: Was the money legally available for that purpose, and does the spending follow the rules that govern it (1971 Act)
The 'wisdom, faithfulness and economy' of spending; can comment on waste and extravagance
Economy, efficiency and effectiveness: did the programme achieve its aims, and at what cost. Confirmed as within CAG's scope by a Finance Ministry Office Memorandum of 2006
Within his scope; he CAN do it
Extra audit done by the CAG on companies or corporations that private auditors have already checked

blocks.title: The three annual reports to the President
head: Report
What it shows
rows: Actual spending compared with sums sanctioned by Parliament through the Appropriation Act
Annual receipts and payments (disbursements) of the Union

blocks.title: Accountability chain for a report on Union accounts

steps.step: 1. CAG submits report to the President
2. President has it laid before both Houses of Parliament
3. Public Accounts Committee (PAC) examines it
steps.detail: Reports on public undertakings go to the Committee on Public Undertakings.

steps.step: 4. PAC reports its findings to Parliament (Lok Sabha)
steps.detail: Final responsibility to act on the CAG's comments lies with Parliament.

blocks.title: CAG and the PAC
items: The CAG is NOT a member or chairman of the PAC. He assists it and attends its sittings, so he is its 'guide, friend and philosopher'.
The PAC examines CAG reports; the Estimates Committee does not.
The PAC does not direct the CAG's work and cannot remove him.
The PAC has 22 members: 15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha. It is NOT '25 members from Lok Sabha alone'.

blocks.title: Why CAG reports matter beyond audit
items: PAC discusses CAG reports on how ministries carried out projects and programmes.
Investigating agencies can use information in CAG reports to charge people who broke the law in handling public money.
CAG reports exposed the 2G spectrum allocation, coal block allocation and Commonwealth Games irregularities. The Harshad Mehta securities scam (1992) was NOT a CAG exposure.
The CAG has no exchequer control (power to stop money being released), even in an emergency, and no judicial powers.

blocks.text: Note: the CAG framed auditing standards for social audit under MGNREGA (the rural job guarantee scheme). Social audit means the local people themselves check the scheme's work and spending. These standards were sent to all States in December 2016.

blocks.title: Indian CAG vs British CAG
head: Aspect
India
Britain
rows: Only Auditor-General, though the Constitution calls him Comptroller too
None. Departments draw money by cheques without his permission
Executive can draw money from the exchequer only with his approval
His audit comes only after the money is spent, so it is called a 'post-mortem' (examination after the event)

blocks.title: Other limits
items: Secret service expenditure: he cannot ask for details. He must accept a certificate from the competent authority that the money was spent under its authority.

More freedom over expenditure audit than over receipts, stores and stock. For expenditure he decides the scope and writes his own audit codes and manuals; for receipts, stores and stock he needs the executive government's approval for the rules.

Integrated audit machinery: one CAG audits both Centre and States, but the President appoints and removes him without consulting the States. So it limits States' financial autonomy and is counted as a unitary (non-federal) feature. The US Comptroller-General has no role in state accounts.

blocks.title: Public corporations: three audit patterns
head: Pattern
Example (from older Laxmikanth editions)
rows: Audited fully and directly by the CAG
Damodar Valley Corporation, ONGC, Air India
Private auditors appointed by the Central Government in consultation with the CAG; CAG may do supplementary audit
Central Warehousing Corporation, Industrial Finance Corporation
Wholly private audit; CAG has no role; reports go straight to Parliament
Life Insurance Corporation, Reserve Bank of India, State Bank of India
blocks.note: Government companies: audited by private auditors appointed by the government on the CAG's advice; CAG can do supplementary or test audit.

V. Narahari Rao becomes the first CAG of independent India
Constitution comes into force with Article 148
Paul H. Appleby's two reports criticise the CAG
CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act passed
Accounts separated from audit for the Union Government (CAG stops compiling Union accounts)
Finance Ministry memo: performance audit is within CAG's scope
K. Sanjay Murthy takes over as CAG (first Telugu officer in the post)

blocks.title: CAGs to remember
head: CAG
Note
rows: Second CAG; later praised the PAC
Present CAG, since November 2024 (as of Nov 2026)

blocks.title: Who said what
head: Person
View
rows: CAG is the most important officer under the Constitution
Paul H. Appleby (American public administration scholar)

Audit is 'a necessary, but a highly pedestrian function' (dull, routine) with limited usefulness. He said CAG work is a colonial inheritance and makes officers afraid to decide. He even suggested relieving the CAG of audit, in other words abolishing the office (not expanding its powers).

blocks.title: Challenges noted by the 2nd Administrative Reforms Commission (2009)
items: The Public Accounts Committee examines in detail only about 15–20 of the 1000–1500 paragraphs (audit points) in CAG reports each year.
Audit is post facto (after the event), so findings often come too late.
Findings rely only on files and papers, with almost no physical checking on the ground. Reports are also seen as too negative (fault-finding).
6 years OR 65 years, whichever is earlier. Not 5 years, not 60.
Removed like a Supreme Court judge: by the President, after both Houses pass a resolution by special majority. He does NOT hold office at the President's pleasure.
Salary is fixed by Parliament (equal to a Supreme Court judge) and charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, so Parliament does not vote on it and no cut motion can reduce it.
Form of accounts: President on CAG's advice (Article 150). Net proceeds: CAG's certificate is final (Article 279).
State reports go to the Governor; Union reports go to the President. The Public Accounts Committee then examines them.
CAG is not a PAC member; no minister (not even the Finance Minister) represents him in Parliament.
Since 1976 he does not compile Union accounts, but still compiles State accounts.
In practice he is only an Auditor-General: unlike the British CAG, he has no control over money leaving the Consolidated Fund.

subcards.title: Attorney General (Art 76), Solicitor General and Advocate General (Art 165)
subcards.summary: The government's top lawyers at the Centre and in each State, and their rights.
at_a_glance: Article 76 — highest law officer of India
Article 165 — highest law officer of a State
AG: fit to be a Supreme Court judge. Advocate General: fit to be a High Court judge
Not fixed by the Constitution. AG holds office during the pleasure (wish) of the President; Advocate General during the pleasure of the Governor
Can speak, but cannot vote (Article 88 for AG in Parliament, Article 177 for Advocate General in the State Legislature)
Second law officer of India; not in the Constitution; assists the AG
AG R. Venkataramani; Solicitor General Tushar Mehta; AP Advocate General Dammalapati Srinivas

sections.heading: Attorney General: appointment, term and pay

blocks.text: Article 76 creates the office of the Attorney General for India. He is the highest law officer of the country (also called the 'first law officer' of India). Article 76 is in Part V (The Union), Chapter I (The Executive), so the AG is part of the Union executive.

blocks.title: Appointment and term
head: Point
Rule
rows: The President, under Article 76(1). In practice, the President acts on the advice of the Union Council of Ministers.
Must be qualified to be appointed a judge of the Supreme Court.

A citizen of India AND one of these: (a) a High Court judge for 5 years, or (b) an advocate of a High Court for 10 years, or (c) a distinguished (eminent) jurist — a respected legal scholar — in the opinion of the President.
The Constitution gives no procedure and no grounds for removal. He holds office during the pleasure of the President, so the President can remove him at any time. Parliament plays no part.
He writes his resignation to the President.
He resigns when the government (Union council of ministers) resigns or is replaced, because he was appointed on its advice. The Constitution itself does NOT require this.

Not fixed by the Constitution. He gets whatever pay the President decides. Parliament does not fix it. It is also not 'charged' on the Consolidated Fund of India (paid without a vote of Parliament), unlike the CAG's salary.

blocks.title: Term in practice (as of Nov 2026)
items: R. Venkataramani (16th AG) was appointed in 2022 for three years.
He was re-appointed for two more years from 1 October 2025 (till 30 September 2027).
This shows the term is decided by the government, not by the Constitution.

sections.heading: Attorney General: duties, rights and limits

blocks.title: Duties under Article 76
head: Duty
Who gives it
rows: Advise the Government of India on legal matters
Matters referred to him by the President
Do other duties of a legal character
Duties assigned by the President (not the Prime Minister)
Do functions given by the Constitution or any other law

blocks.title: Duties assigned by the President (notification of 26 January 1950)
head: Duty
rows: Appear for the Government of India in all Supreme Court cases in which it is concerned.
Represent the Government of India in a reference by the President to the Supreme Court under Article 143 (when the President asks the Supreme Court for its advisory opinion).
Appear in any High Court case concerning the Government of India — only when the Government asks him to, not in every case.

blocks.title: Rights
head: Right
Detail
rows: Right of audience (right to be heard as a lawyer)
In ALL courts in the territory of India, not only the Supreme Court. So he can appear even in a district court.
Can speak and take part in both Houses, their joint sitting, and any parliamentary committee he is named a member of. He CANNOT vote anywhere.
Gets all the privileges and immunities of an MP, such as freedom of speech in Parliament.
He is not a member of Parliament.

blocks.title: Limitations (to avoid conflict of duty)
head: He should not…
rows: advise or hold a brief (take a case) against the Government of India.

advise or take a case for anyone else in a matter where he is asked to advise or appear for the Government. Example: a private company asks him for advice in a case where he appears for the Government — he must decline.
defend accused persons in criminal cases WITHOUT the Government of India's permission. (With permission he can.)
become a director of a company or corporation WITHOUT the Government of India's permission.
advise any Union ministry, department, statutory body or public sector undertaking unless the request comes through the Ministry of Law and Justice, Department of Legal Affairs.

blocks.title: Position of the AG
items: He is NOT a full-time counsel for the Government.
He is NOT a government servant.
So he is NOT barred from private legal practice (he can take private cases, within the limits above).
He is NOT a member of the Union Cabinet or council of ministers. A separate Law Minister handles legal matters at the political level.
In the USA, the Attorney General IS a Cabinet member with executive power — India is different.

Contempt of Court: under section 15 of the Contempt of Courts Act 1971, a private person can ask the Supreme Court to start a criminal contempt case (for example, for scandalising or lowering the authority of the court) only with the written consent of the AG or the Solicitor General. The Supreme Court can also start such a case on its own (suo motu).

blocks.title: Law officers of the Union
head: Rank
Office
Key fact

Assist the AG. NOT mentioned in the Constitution.
blocks.note: Article 76 mentions only the AG. Only the AG's office is created by the Constitution.

items: The Solicitor General is appointed by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (a committee of the Union Cabinet that approves top appointments). He is NOT appointed by the President under any Article of the Constitution.

The Solicitor General has no right to speak in Parliament. Article 88 gives this right only to Ministers and the AG. So the statement 'the AG and the Solicitor General are the only officers allowed in Parliament' is wrong.
States have no 'Solicitor General'. The Solicitor General is a Union officer.
First Solicitor General: C.K. Daphtary (he later became the 2nd AG).
Current Solicitor General: Tushar Mehta, re-appointed for three years from 1 July 2026 (as of Nov 2026).

Public Prosecutor: appointed under the criminal procedure law (section 24 of the CrPC, now section 18 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) 2023) to conduct cases for the State in criminal courts. It is not a constitutional post.

Not a constitutional post; assists the AG

blocks.text: Article 165 (Part VI, The States, Chapter 2, The Executive) creates the office of the Advocate General. He is the highest law officer in the State — the State's version of the AG. He is part of the State executive, but NOT a member of the State council of ministers.

blocks.title: Rules
head: Point
Rule
rows: The Governor (not the President on the Governor's advice).
Must be qualified to be a High Court judge: a citizen of India AND either (a) held a judicial office for 10 years, or (b) an advocate of a High Court for 10 years.
An office in the judicial service of the State (for example, a district judge or civil judge).
The Constitution has no provision to appoint an eminent jurist as a High Court judge, so this route is not available for the Advocate General either.
Not fixed by the Constitution (no five-year term).

No procedure or grounds in the Constitution. He holds office during the pleasure of the Governor, so the Governor can remove him at any time. When the Governor withdraws his pleasure, he ceases to hold office. No address by the legislature is needed.

By custom (not a written rule), he resigns when the State council of ministers resigns or is replaced — for example, when a new party wins the Assembly election — because he was appointed on its advice.
Whatever the Governor decides (Article 165(3)) — not fixed by the State Legislature.

blocks.title: Duties and rights
head: Item
Detail
rows: Advise the State government on legal matters referred to him by the Governor.
Do other legal duties assigned by the Governor (not by the Chief Justice of the High Court).
Do functions given by the Constitution or any other law.
Giving advisory opinions to the High Court. (High Courts have no advisory jurisdiction at all.)
Can speak and take part in both Houses of the State Legislature (Assembly and Council) and any committee he is named to — but CANNOT vote.
Gets all privileges and immunities of a member of the State Legislature.
As the State's highest law officer, he can appear for the State government, for example in a suit in a district court.
blocks.note: His right to take part in the proceedings comes from Article 177. Article 194 only gives him privileges (special protections); it is not the source of this right.

items: The AG must be qualified to be a Supreme Court judge; the Advocate General must be qualified to be a High Court judge. Only the AG can be appointed as an 'eminent jurist' (distinguished legal scholar).
Neither has a fixed term. Both serve at the pleasure of the President or Governor. Resigning with the government is a convention, not a constitutional rule.
Pay: the President decides the AG's pay and the Governor decides the Advocate General's pay. Parliament or the State Legislature does not fix it.
The AG has the right of audience (right to be heard as a lawyer) in ALL courts of India, not only the Supreme Court.
AG and Advocate General can speak in the legislature and sit on committees, but can never vote (Art 88, Art 177).

sections.heading: The three commissions at a glance

blocks.text: NCSC, NCST and NCBC are constitutional bodies: an Article of the Constitution itself creates each one, so only a constitutional amendment can abolish them. Bodies like the National Commission for Women (1992), the National Commission for Minorities (1993), the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC, 1993) and the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR, 2007) are only statutory bodies (created by an ordinary Act of Parliament).

blocks.title: Where these Articles sit
items: Art 330 to Art 342A form Part XVI of the Constitution, titled 'Special provisions relating to certain classes'. These classes are Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), backward classes and Anglo-Indians.

Art 335 (also in Part XVI): the claims of SCs and STs must be taken into account when making appointments to Union and state government services, as long as efficiency of administration is maintained.
Art 341 gives the list of Scheduled Castes. Art 342 gives the list of Scheduled Tribes. Art 342A gives the list of socially and educationally backward classes (SEBCs).

For Art 341 and Art 342, the President notifies the list for a state after consulting its Governor. Only Parliament, by law, can later include or exclude a caste or tribe – not a fresh Presidential notification.

sections.heading: How the SC and ST commissions evolved

blocks.title: From one officer to two commissions

items.what: Original Art 338: a single Special Officer for SCs and STs
items.detail: He was called the Commissioner for SCs and STs. He investigated how the constitutional safeguards (protections) for SCs and STs were working and reported to the President (not to Parliament).

items.what: A multi-member Commission for SCs and STs with no law behind it (non-statutory)
items.detail: Set up by a government Resolution (no law behind it). Chaired by Bhola Paswan Shastri. The Commissioner for SCs and STs also continued.

items.what: Renamed 'National Commission for SCs and STs'
items.detail: Done by another Resolution, which changed its functions. It was still only a national-level advisory body, without statutory or constitutional status.

items.what: 65th Amendment: a multi-member National Commission for SCs and STs under Art 338, with constitutional status
items.detail: It replaced BOTH the single Commissioner for SCs and STs AND the 1987 Resolution commission. First chairperson: S.H. Ram Dhan.

items.what: Separate Ministry of Tribal Affairs created
items.detail: Reason: STs differ from SCs in where they live and in culture, so their problems are different. The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment could not coordinate all ST matters well.

items.what: 89th Amendment: the joint commission split into two
items.detail: It amended Art 338 (now NCSC only) and inserted a new Art 338A (NCST). It did NOT insert Art 338B.

blocks.title: Six functions (same wording for NCSC, NCST and NCBC)
head: Function
rows: Investigate and monitor all matters about the constitutional and other legal safeguards (protections) for the group, and judge how well they work
Inquire into specific complaints that the group was denied its rights and safeguards
Take part in, and advise on, planning for the group's social and economic development, and judge the progress made under the Union or a state
Present reports to the President every year, and at other times when it thinks fit
Recommend steps the Union or a state should take to implement the safeguards and for welfare and development
Do any other work for the group's protection, welfare and development that the President assigns
blocks.note: The commissions are watchdogs and advisers. Their recommendations are NOT binding, and they do not run schemes or administer Scheduled Areas.

Preventing alienation (loss) of tribal land, and rehabilitating those who already lost it
Involving tribal communities in protecting forests and social afforestation
Full implementation of the PESA Act, 1996 (Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas)
Reducing and finally ending shifting cultivation (clearing a forest patch, farming it for a few years, then moving on)

steps.step: Commission presents the report to the President
steps.detail: Every year, and also whenever it thinks necessary.

steps.step: President places it before Parliament
steps.detail: With a memorandum explaining action taken on each recommendation and reasons for not accepting any.

steps.step: Report about a state is sent onward
steps.detail: NCSC and NCST: President sends it to the state Governor, who places it before the state legislature with an action-taken memorandum. NCBC: President sends it to the state government (not the Governor) – Art 338B(7).

blocks.title: Powers (same for all three)
head: Power
Detail
rows: Each commission can decide its own procedure (how it conducts its work)
While investigating a matter or inquiring into a complaint, it has all powers of a civil court trying a suit

(1) summon any person from any part of India and question him on oath; (2) order that any document be found and produced; (3) accept evidence given on affidavits (sworn written statements); (4) call for any public record from any court or office; (5) issue summons to examine witnesses and documents; (6) any other matter the President decides
The Union and every state government must consult it on all major policy matters affecting the group. They must only consult it; they do not need its approval.

blocks.title: Extra groups covered by NCSC
items: Art 338(10): wherever Art 338 mentions Scheduled Castes, it also includes the Anglo-Indian community. So NCSC also watches over the safeguards for Anglo-Indians.
Till 2018, NCSC also looked after the backward classes (Other Backward Classes, OBCs). The 102nd Amendment (2018) removed this duty, because NCBC took it over.

items.what: Indra Sawhney case (Mandal case)
items.detail: Supreme Court told the Centre and the state governments to create permanent bodies to examine complaints of under-inclusion, over-inclusion or non-inclusion of any class in the backward classes lists. NCBC at the Centre and state Backward Classes Commissions (like Andhra Pradesh's) followed.

items.what: NCBC set up as a statutory body
items.detail: Under the National Commission for Backward Classes Act, 1993.

items.what: 102nd Amendment: NCBC becomes constitutional (Art 338B)
items.detail: Its functions were widened, and its status is now equal to NCSC and NCST. The 1993 Act was repealed (cancelled) by the NCBC (Repeal) Act, 2018. The amendment also inserted Art 342A, which lets the President specify the socially and educationally backward classes (SEBCs).

items.what: Ram Singh case: Jats removed from the Central OBC List
items.detail: Supreme Court quashed the notification that had added the Jat community to the Central List of OBCs.

items.what: Maratha reservation case (Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil case)
items.detail: Supreme Court struck down the Maratha quota because it crossed the 50% ceiling on reservation. It also read Art 342A as taking away the states' power to identify SEBCs. It did not strike down Art 342A itself.

items.what: 105th Amendment restores states' power
items.detail: States and Union Territories may again prepare and keep their own SEBC lists for their own purposes.

blocks.title: Art 342A after the 105th Amendment
head: Point
Rule
rows: The President specifies the SEBCs in the Central List, which is used for central government purposes. For a state, the President does this after consulting its Governor.
Only Parliament, by law. A later Presidential notification cannot change it.
The SEBC list prepared and maintained by and for the central government
A state or Union Territory may prepare and keep its own SEBC list, which may differ from the Central List. A state does this by a law of its own legislature, not of Parliament.
States need NOT consult NCBC when preparing their own SEBC list. The 105th Amendment gave them this exemption.

blocks.text: Art 340: the President MAY appoint a commission to investigate the conditions of socially and educationally backward classes and recommend steps to improve them. Its report is placed before Parliament with a memorandum on the action taken. Art 340 is only about such inquiry commissions; it does NOT create NCBC (NCBC comes from Art 338B).

A linguistic minority is a group whose mother tongue is different from the main language of the state (or of part of a state). It is decided state by state: for example, Telugu speakers are a linguistic minority in Karnataka. A language need not be in the Eighth Schedule for its speakers to count as a linguistic minority.

blocks.text: State commissions for SCs, STs and BCs are statutory bodies: each is created by a law of the State Legislature, not by the Constitution. Their members are appointed by the state government, not by the President.

blocks.title: AP BC Commission – key points
items: The state government must consult it when revising the state BC lists (revision at least once every 10 years).
Its advice is not binding: the government lays an action-taken memorandum, with reasons for not accepting any advice, before the Legislative Assembly.
First chairman: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (1994–2003).

Amendment order: the 65th Amendment (1990) created the multi-member commission for SCs and STs; the 89th (2003) split it into two; the 102nd (2018) made NCBC constitutional; the 105th (2021) gave states back their own SEBC lists.
Articles: Art 338 is NCSC; Art 338A is NCST; Art 338B is NCBC; Art 340 is the inquiry commission on backward classes; Art 350B is the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.
Term and service conditions are fixed by the President, not by the Constitution or by Parliament: 3 years, and no one can serve more than 2 terms.
NCBC state reports go to the state government; NCSC and NCST state reports go to the Governor.
Governments must CONSULT the commissions; recommendations are not binding.
NCSC also covers the Anglo-Indian community (Art 338(10)). Its role for OBCs ended in 2018.
The National Commission for Women, National Commission for Minorities, NHRC and NCPCR are statutory. NCSC, NCST, NCBC and the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities are constitutional.

Art 350B is in Part XVII and was inserted in 1956. The office began in 1957. The Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities (CLM) works under the Ministry of Minority Affairs, with headquarters in New Delhi.
State SC, ST and BC commissions (e.g. in Andhra Pradesh) are statutory, made by state laws; the national ones are constitutional.
